\chapter{One Word, and a Whole Sentence After It}
\label{ch:ru-chto}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask what, say I think that something is so, say what it is I do not know, and write the dash that stands where the missing verb to be would have been.}

chto is the cheapest sentence-level word in the queue: one syllable that turns dumat and znat -- both taught chapters ago and both stuck without an object -- into verbs that carry a whole clause. It is also the word Russian spells with a ch and says with a sh in one job and not the other, and the word English splits into that and what while Russian does not. The chapter ends on the dash, which is the only mark in the language whose job is to stand in for a word the sentence never says.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[shto]{\ru{что} — \textquotedblleft{}what,\textquotedblright{} spelled with a \ru{ч} and said with a sh}

\label{lesson:RU-C18-chto-vopros}



\begin{quote}
Two parts of the face, and the mark that closes a question.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{нос}}, inherited straight from the root behind English \emph{nose}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{рот}}, probably from a verb meaning \textbf{to dig} — a snout rooting the ground
  \item \emph{Recall:} the one question mark at the \textbf{end}, and \emph{\ru{но}}, the \emph{but} with no cousin
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{что}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{что}} — \emph{shto} — \textbf{what}
\end{itemize}

Read the spelling and then read the sound again, because they disagree. The word is written with \textbf{\ru{ч}}, and it is said with a \textbf{\ru{ш}}: \emph{shto}, never \emph{chto}.

That is not carelessness. It is one of a small handful of Russian words where the old spelling was kept after the pronunciation moved, and it is the commonest of them, so it is worth learning as a fact about this word rather than as a rule.

\textbf{\ru{что}?} on its own is already a whole question, and it is the plainest way to ask somebody to say a word again. A single word, a rising voice, and one mark at the end.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{что}} goes back to PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}id}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{} — the same word as Latin \textbf{quid} and English \textbf{what} itself.

You have met this family before. The farewell \textbf{\ru{пока}} was built on the ancient question-stem \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-}, the one behind \textbf{\ru{как}} and the entire English \emph{wh-} set. \textbf{\ru{что}} is that family's plainest member, and the book collects the rest of it over the chapters that follow.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\ru{что}} — \emph{shto}, with a \textbf{\ru{ш}} sound and a \textbf{\ru{ч}} on the page
  \item it as a one-word question, voice rising
  \item the three you own — \emph{\ru{как}}, \emph{\ru{пока}}, \emph{\ru{что}} — one ancient stem
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}what.\textquotedblright{} (It is \textbf{\ru{что}}, said \emph{shto}.) Which letter is on the page and which sound comes out? (\textbf{\ru{ч}} on the page, \textbf{\ru{ш}} in the mouth.) Which two words you already own belong to the same ancient family? (They are \textbf{\ru{как}} and \textbf{\ru{пока}}.) And one look back: which part of the face is a straight inheritance from the root behind \emph{nose}? (That is \textbf{\ru{нос}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[…, shto …]{\ru{что} as a hinge — one word carrying a whole sentence}

\label{lesson:RU-C18-chto-soyuz}



\begin{quote}
Two more of the body, and the newest word in the book.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{глаз}}, which began as slang for a \textbf{ball} and pushed the true eye-word out of the language
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{сердце}}, English \emph{heart} barely disguised, and the letter \textbf{\ru{ц}} inside it
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{что}} said \emph{shto}, and \emph{\ru{а}}, the \emph{whereas} word
  \item \emph{Recall:} the first letters you wrote — \textbf{\ru{р} \ru{с} \ru{н} \ru{б} \ru{д} \ru{е} \ru{т}} — and the one that looks like an English R and is not one
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the same word, doing the other job}]
Put \textbf{\ru{что}} between two clauses instead of at the front of a question, and it stops asking and starts carrying:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{знаю}, \ru{что} \ru{ты} \ru{понимаешь}} — \emph{ya znáyu, shto ty panimáyesh} — I know \textbf{that} you understand.
\end{itemize}

Three things to notice, and the third is the one to hold on to.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item The \textbf{comma is compulsory}. Russian puts one in front of \textbf{\ru{что}} every single time, with no exceptions of the kind English allows.
  \item The English \emph{that} can be dropped — \emph{I know you understand} is perfectly good English. The Russian \textbf{\ru{что}} cannot. Leave it out and the sentence breaks.
  \item As a joining word it is said the way it is \textbf{spelled}: \emph{chto}, not \emph{shto}. Same letters, two jobs, two pronunciations.
\end{itemize}

English plays the same trick, twice: \emph{what} and \emph{that} both began as question words and one of them settled into this job.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{знаю}, \ru{что} \ru{ты} \ru{понимаешь}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{что}} twice — as the question \emph{shto}, then as the hinge \emph{chto}
  \item \emph{Build:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{знаю}, \ru{что}} plus any sentence you can already make
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
May the Russian \textbf{\ru{что}} be dropped the way English drops \emph{that}? (\textbf{No} — never.) What must always stand in front of it? (\textbf{A comma}.) Which of the two jobs is said \emph{shto}? (\textbf{The question}.) And one look back: which eye-word did \emph{\ru{глаз}} push out of everyday Russian? (The word \textbf{\ru{око}}, which survives inside \emph{\ru{очки}}, \textquotedblleft{}little eyes.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ya dúmayu, shto …]{\ru{я} \ru{думаю}, \ru{что} … — saying that an opinion is yours}

\label{lesson:RU-C18-dumayu-chto}



\begin{quote}
The two farewells, formal and casual, and the number from the last chapter.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{до} \ru{свидания}}, literally \textbf{until the re-seeing}, with \emph{\ru{до}} taking the genitive after it
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{пока}}, whose root is ancient and whose use as a goodbye is a hundred years old
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{один}}, and the five English words its root became
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{как} \ru{вас} \ru{зовут}?}, and the choice between \emph{\ru{ты}} and \emph{\ru{вы}} inside it
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the opinion frame}]
\textbf{\ru{думать}} has been in this book since the verbs of the mind, and until this chapter it had nothing to think \textbf{about} — no object bigger than a single word could be attached to it. \textbf{\ru{что}} fixes that in one move:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{думаю}, \ru{что} …} — \emph{ya dúmayu, shto …} — \textbf{I think that …}
\end{itemize}

Whatever you can already say in Russian, you can now say you \textbf{think} it. That is a genuine step up rather than one more phrase: it turns every sentence you own into an opinion you have marked as your own, which is the difference between reporting a fact and taking a position.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{думаю}, \ru{что} \ru{ты} \ru{понимаешь}} — \emph{ya dúmayu, shto ty panimáyesh} — I think that you understand.
\end{itemize}

The comma before \textbf{\ru{что}} is compulsory here as everywhere.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{думаю}, \ru{что} \ru{ты} \ru{понимаешь}}
  \item \emph{Build:} take any sentence you own and put \emph{\ru{я} \ru{думаю}, \ru{что}} in front of it
  \item \emph{Build:} the same sentence without the frame, and hear it turn back into a flat claim
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I think that you understand.\textquotedblright{} (That is \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{думаю}, \ru{что} \ru{ты} \ru{понимаешь}}.) What had \emph{\ru{думать}} been missing until now? (\textbf{Anything to think about that was bigger than one word}.) Does the comma stay? (\textbf{Yes} — always.) And one look back: what does \emph{\ru{до} \ru{свидания}} literally say? (\textbf{Until the re-seeing}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ya ne znáyu, shto …]{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{знаю}, \ru{что} … — admitting it, in a whole sentence}

\label{lesson:RU-C18-znayu-chto}



\begin{quote}
Two more farewells, and the divider from the last chapter.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{до} \ru{скорого}}, built on a word meaning \textbf{quick} with no English cousin at all
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{до} \ru{завтра}}, and \emph{\ru{завтра}} built on the root behind English \emph{east} and \emph{aurora}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{другой}}, and the split \emph{\ru{один} … \ru{другой} …}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the other frame, and the negative one}]
\textbf{\ru{знать}} takes \textbf{\ru{что}} exactly as \textbf{\ru{думать}} does, and the negative is where it earns its place:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{знаю}, \ru{что} \ru{ты} \ru{понимаешь}} — I know \textbf{that} you understand.
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{знаю}, \ru{что} \ru{ты} \ru{говоришь}} — \emph{ya ne znáyu, shto ty gavarísh} — I do not know \textbf{what} you are saying.
\end{itemize}

Read those two English translations again. The Russian word is \textbf{the same word both times}, and English needs \emph{that} in the first and \emph{what} in the second. Russian makes no such split, which is one distinction fewer for you to get wrong.

The second sentence is the useful one. Until now this book could say \emph{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{знаю}} and stop — a flat shrug. With \textbf{\ru{что}} you can say what it is you do not know, which is what turns an admission into something the other person can act on.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{знаю}, \ru{что} \ru{ты} \ru{говоришь}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the same sentence without \textbf{\ru{не}}, and hear it turn into a claim
  \item \emph{Build:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{знаю}, \ru{что}} plus anything you own
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I do not know what you are saying.\textquotedblright{} (That is \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{знаю}, \ru{что} \ru{ты} \ru{говоришь}}.) How many Russian words cover English's \emph{that} and \emph{what} here? (\textbf{One} — \textbf{\ru{что}} does both.) Which two verbs now take a whole sentence after them? (\textbf{\ru{думать}} and \textbf{\ru{знать}}.) And one look back: which farewell is built on the word for \emph{morning}? (That is \textbf{\ru{до} \ru{завтра}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tire]{— the dash that stands where the verb would have been}

\label{lesson:RU-W09-tire}



\begin{quote}
The last two farewells, and the marks from the previous writing lesson.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{до} \ru{встречи}}, built from \textbf{into} plus \textbf{with} on a root with no secure English cousin
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{спокойной} \ru{ночи}}, whose \emph{\ru{ночь}} is one of the most secure cognates in the family and whose \emph{\ru{покой}} is the root of English \emph{quiet}
  \item \emph{Recall:} the dot at the end, and the single question mark
  \item \emph{Recall:} three letters from the middle of the alphabet — \textbf{\ru{ж}}, \textbf{\ru{ч}}, and the soft sign that makes no sound at all
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — one long stroke on the line}
Russian's dash is \textbf{\ru{тире}}, and it is a genuinely long mark — longer than an English hyphen, with a space on each side of it:

\begin{quote}
\ru{брат} — \ru{друг}
\end{quote}

Draw it at the height of the small letters, not at the top and not on the baseline, and give it the length of about two letters.

The mark is a French loan, \textbf{tiret}, borrowed whole. What Russian does with it is not French at all.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the mark for a verb that is not there}]
You learned early that Russian says \emph{I am a student} with no verb in the middle: the present tense of \textbf{\ru{быть}} is absent altogether. On the page, that absence gets a mark of its own.

Where the sentence would have needed \textbf{is}, and both halves are nouns, a Russian writer puts a dash:

\begin{quote}
\ru{сестра} — \ru{подруга}
\end{quote}

\emph{A sister is a friend.} There is no verb in that sentence and there never will be. The dash is doing its work — and it is the only punctuation mark in the language whose job is to stand in for a word.

Say it aloud and there is a small pause exactly where the dash sits. The mark is not decoration; it is written-down silence.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \emph{\ru{сестра} — \ru{подруга}}, with a space on each side of the dash
  \item \emph{Say it:} the same sentence, and put a small pause where the dash is
  \item \emph{Write it:} one sentence of your own with two nouns and a dash between them
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What word is the dash standing in for? (\textbf{The verb \emph{to be}}, which Russian does not say in the present.) How is it drawn? (\textbf{Long, on the level of the small letters, with a space each side}.) And one look back: which farewell means \emph{calm} plus \emph{night}? (That is \textbf{\ru{спокойной} \ru{ночи}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
